messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Coast Guard
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 69

He is 29, European, and works in the Coast Guard, a job that has trained him to stay alert, read risk quickly, and keep moving when others hesitate. Even so, the robbery that changed him happens in a moment that still feels, to him, strangely ordinary. He is off duty at the time, walking home after a late evening with his girlfriend, when two men step out from a side street and close the distance too fast. One of them keeps his face partly turned away, the other does the talking, demanding his wallet and phone. The patient remembers the sharpness of the voice more than the exact words. He remembers noticing, with a kind of cold disbelief, that his body does not respond the way it does during training. He freezes. He sees the glint of metal and is sure, in the instant before handing over everything, that he is about to be stabbed. The scene ends without a fight, but his body does not know that yet.

In the days after, he keeps replaying the robbery in fragments. He thinks about how quickly it happened, how easily they chose him, and how little control he had once they were close enough to touch. He feels ashamed that he did not resist, ashamed that he later tells people he is “fine” because he cannot bear the look of concern in their faces. At work he becomes hyperaware of his surroundings. As a Coast Guard officer, he is used to scanning water, docks, and crowds for danger, but now the scanning extends to every street, every parking lot, every person moving behind him. He takes longer routes to avoid the place where it happened. He checks windows and doors repeatedly. If someone comes up behind him unexpectedly, he startles so hard it feels embarrassing, almost childish, and then he grows angry with himself for being unable to shake it off.

Sleep becomes broken and unreliable. He falls asleep exhausted, only to wake an hour or two later with his heart racing, already oriented to the fear before he is fully awake. Sometimes he wakes from the same dream: the men approaching, the metal in the hand, his own inability to move. In the dream he tries to shout and nothing comes out. In the mornings he feels drained before the day begins, as if he has spent the night in combat rather than in bed beside his girlfriend. She notices that he is more distant, quicker to irritation, less able to tolerate ordinary interruptions. When she asks what is wrong, he says he is just tired. He hates how often he feels split between wanting comfort and wanting to be left alone.

He also begins to avoid anything that reminds him of the assault. He will not walk on that street, and he does not like being in crowded areas after dark. He notices himself calculating exits in restaurants and transit stations. He does not like the feel of his wallet in his pocket anymore because it reminds him of the moment it was taken. He becomes tense during routine physical contact, even a casual hand on his shoulder. The body he once relied on to stay composed now seems to betray him with sudden surges of panic, tightness in his chest, and a sense that he is never fully off alert. He describes feeling “stuck on watch,” as if his nervous system has stayed behind at the scene while his life has moved on around it.

Over time, the robbery begins to shape how he sees himself. He does not talk about it much, but he thinks about it constantly, especially at work where competence and control matter. He worries that he should have been able to do something different. He compares himself to the version of himself he believes he should be: steadier, tougher, less shaken. Instead, he feels more cautious and more easily cornered. He is still committed to his partner and to his job, and from the outside he can appear functional, even disciplined. But inside, he is organizing his world around danger, measuring distance, watching hands, and bracing for the next sudden approach.
